title: Meta Agrees to Shut Teens Out at Night and During School
hook: Researchers have argued for years that the worst social media harm is what it displaces — sleep and school. Meta has now agreed to cut minors off during exactly those hours.
key_points: Meta agreed to changes for minors on Instagram and Facebook, including overnight and school-day cutoffs.
Researchers and advocates called the two time-based limits the most significant part.
Late-night scrolling displaces sleep, which teens need more of than adults.
School-day access fragments attention during the hours meant for learning.
Platform-level defaults reach far more teens than parent-by-parent rules do.
Time limits address when teens use the apps, not what the feed shows them.
content_html: Meta has agreed to a set of changes for minors on Instagram and Facebook, and researchers and advocates who study adolescent mental health picked out the same two as the ones that count: teens get cut off overnight, and during the school day.
extra_html:
Both are time-based rather than content-based, which fits what the research has been saying. A recurring finding in this area is that social media does much of its damage by displacement — the hour of scrolling at 1am is an hour of sleep that adolescents, who need more of it than adults, don't get. The school-day cutoff targets the other big displacement: attention during the hours built for learning. Neither requires anyone to settle the harder argument about whether the content itself is harmful.

The other reason experts are encouraged is reach. A platform default applies to every minor at once, including the many whose households have no realistic way to enforce a phone rule. What the changes don't touch is the feed itself — what teens see, and how hard it pulls, during all the hours they're still allowed to be there.

related.title: Building Healthier Screen Habits
related.hook: You don't need to quit your phone — just out-design it. A few small tweaks beat willpower for taking back your attention.

related.title: Screens and Your Wellbeing
related.hook: It's not just how many hours you're on a screen — it's how and when. The same phone can leave you rested or wrecked depending on use.

related.title: When Scrolling Stops Being a Habit
related.hook: Losing sleep to your phone isn't automatically an addiction — but there's a line, and courts are now arguing over who put it there.

related.title: Building Better Sleep Habits
related.hook: Good sleep is mostly built in the hours before bed. A handful of simple habits — collectively called sleep hygiene — do more than any gadget.

flashcards.prompt: Which two changes did researchers single out as the big ones?

choices.text: Cutting teens off overnight and during the school day
Removing all advertising from teen accounts
Requiring a parent to approve every post

flashcards.explanation_html: Both are time-based. They target the hours social media most directly displaces — sleep at night, and attention during school.

flashcards.prompt: Why do platform-level defaults matter more than household rules?
flashcards.back_html: A default applies to every minor on the platform at once, including teens whose parents can't police devices. Household rules only reach one family at a time.

flashcards.prompt: What do time limits not address?
flashcards.back_html: What the feed shows. Restricting when a teen can scroll says nothing about the content, comparison pressure or algorithmic pull during the hours they can.
